title: Walking, again
hookLine: every walk is a crusade to reconquer the Holy Land (Walking)

cards: Back in year one, this path met Thoreau the saunterer, the man who could walk for hours with no errand. Today, back to the same essay, Walking, read this time for its nerve.
Underneath the strolling, Thoreau makes outrageous demands. To take a walk properly, you must be ready never to come home. A walk can be a sort of crusade.
He even has opinions about which way to turn when you leave the house.

teach.h: EVERY WALK A SORT OF CRUSADE.
teach.b: First, the crusade. Thoreau writes that "every walk is a sort of crusade," stirred up by some preacher inside us, to go out and win back a holy land.
It's a borrowed image from the medieval wars, and an uneasy one to hear today. But the land he means to win back is the ground he walks: the woods and fields outside town.

teach.h: READY NEVER TO SEE THEM AGAIN.
teach.b: Second, the readiness: "If you are ready to leave father and mother, and brother and sister, and wife and child and friends, and never see them again,—if you have paid your debts, and made your will, and settled all your affairs, and are a free man, then you are ready for a walk."
It's a joke, and it isn't. Don't walk while still half at your desk.

Third, the shortest walk: "We should go forth on the shortest walk, perchance, in the spirit of undying adventure, never to return." The adventure isn't in the distance. It's in the spirit you carry out the door.
Fourth, the direction. Stepping outside, not yet sure where he's going, he finds himself settling southwest, toward some wood or meadow. The future lies that way, he says.
"Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free." So walking again doesn't mean the same loop. It means going out as if this street were a frontier.

how: Readers of Thoreau's Walking often take it as an invitation to treat even a short walk as an adventure: leaving errands behind and choosing an unfamiliar way.

o: Thoreau's essay: even a short walk taken as an adventure
a doctor's advice to walk an hour every day for health
a guide to the trails around Concord and Walden Pond

p: in the spirit of undying adventure

s: Thoreau says a real walk has to be a long one
he says even the shortest walk, in the spirit of undying adventure.
Thoreau says he goes east only by force
"eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free."
Thoreau says you're ready for a walk once your shoes are on
he says, half joking, you're ready once you've settled all your affairs and are a free man.

games.q: you step outside with no plan, and stand undecided. which way does Thoreau say something in him turns?
o: southwest, toward some wood or meadow.
games.why: he settles southwest, where the future lies for him. "eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free."

practice: If you can move, take a slow walk right where you are, but go a way you never go: the far end of the hall, a door you don't usually use; if you're sitting, walk in your mind down a nearby street you've never turned down.
Leave your errands behind, as if you'd settled all your affairs. Notice one thing you've never noticed.
